title: Partial Orders and Posets
quickIdea: A partial order is a relation that is reflexive, antisymmetric and transitive. It ranks some pairs of a set without ever forcing a choice between the rest, which is why it is called partial.
remember: A relation R on a set A is a partial order when it is reflexive (aRa for every a), antisymmetric (aRb and bRa together force a = b) and transitive (aRb and bRc force aRc). The pair (A, R) is then a poset.
Antisymmetric is not 'not symmetric': the identity relation is both at once. It only forbids two different elements pointing at each other.
The four standing examples: divisibility on the positive integers, subset inclusion on a power set, 'less than or equal to' on the reals, and the pointwise order on functions into {0, 1}.
'Less than' on the reals is transitive and antisymmetric but not reflexive, so it is not a partial order - a favourite one-mark distractor.
Write a <= b instead of aRb once the relation is known to be a partial order. A total order is the special case where every two elements are comparable.
Every partial order on a finite set is its own transitive closure of the covering pairs, which is exactly why the Hasse diagram loses no information.
Counting: there are 19 partial orders on a 3-element set and 219 on a 4-element set, so brute-force enumeration is not a GATE method - use the axioms.

example.prompt: Show that divisibility on {1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12} is a partial order, and name one pair that is incomparable.
example.work: Reflexive: every number divides itself. Antisymmetric: if a divides b and b divides a then a = b, for positive integers. Transitive: if a divides b and b divides c then a divides c. So it is a partial order. Now 4 and 6: neither divides the other, and 4 does not appear among the multiples of 6 either, so the pair (4, 6) is incomparable.
example.answer: Divisibility is a partial order on these six numbers, and 4 and 6 are incomparable, so the order is partial and not total.

gateAngle: GATE almost never asks you to prove the axioms; it asks which of several relations is a partial order, or how many pairs must be added to reach a total order. Test the three axioms in the cheapest order: reflexivity first (one counterexample kills it), then antisymmetry, then transitivity.

variations.label: CONCEPTUAL PRACTICE QUESTION
variations.question: Is the relation 'a divides b' a partial order on the set of all integers, including 0 and the negatives?
variations.answer: No. On all the integers antisymmetry fails, because 2 divides -2 and -2 divides 2 while 2 is not -2.
variations.why: The divisibility order is a partial order on the positive integers only. Extending the set to all integers breaks antisymmetry, which is the axiom students check last and forget.

variations.label: ORIGINAL PYQ-STYLE QUESTION
variations.question: There are 19 partial orders on the set {1, 2, 3}. How many of them are total orders?
variations.answer: 6 - one for each ordering of the three elements.
variations.why: A total order on a finite set is a linear arrangement, so the total orders are in bijection with the 3! permutations. The other 13 partial orders leave at least one pair incomparable.

variations.label: PREDICTED VARIATION
variations.question: A relation on a 3-element set is reflexive, antisymmetric and transitive except that one element is not related to itself. Is it a partial order, and what is the cheapest repair?
variations.answer: Not a partial order; adding that one pair (a, a) makes it one, because reflexivity is the only missing axiom.
variations.why: A relation missing one diagonal pair can still be antisymmetric and transitive. GATE tests exactly this gap: name the axiom, not the property list.

trap.what: Treating 'antisymmetric' as the negation of 'symmetric', and treating a partial order as a ranking with no ties.
trap.why: Antisymmetry forbids a two-way arrow between different elements; symmetry requires it. The identity relation satisfies both. And a partial order leaves whole pairs unranked - that is the 'partial' in the name.
trap.counterexample: On {1, 2}, the relation {(1,1), (2,2)} is symmetric, antisymmetric and a partial order. The relation {(1,1), (2,2), (1,2), (2,1)} is symmetric but not antisymmetric, so it is not a partial order.

check.question: How many partial orders are there on a 2-element set {a, b}, and how many of them are total orders?
check.answer: 3 partial orders, of which 2 are total orders.
check.explanation: Both reflexive pairs are forced. The pair (a,b) is in or out and the pair (b,a) is in or out, but antisymmetry forbids both: so neither (the identity, a partial order that is not total), (a,b) only, or (b,a) only. That is 3 partial orders and 2 total orders.
